name: Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque
label: Sultan Qaboos Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1721989476: the OpenStreetMap point 'Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque'.
notes: Muscat's most famous landmark, with a huge prayer hall and a courtyard of arches.

text.description:
The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque is the largest mosque in Oman. It was finished in 2001 and can hold up to 20,000 worshippers across its prayer halls, courtyards and passageways. It was inaugurated on 4 May 2001, thirty years into Sultan Qaboos's reign. It was built from about 270,000 tonnes of imported Indian sandstone.

For a phone photo, the outer marble courtyard is the place to start. From there the central dome and the tallest minaret can sit in one frame, with plenty of bright sky above. The main minaret is 90 metres high and the four flanking minarets are 45.5 metres, so the skyline has a pleasing rhythm of tall and short towers. The long pools give a second classic picture, with the dome and minarets reflected and the full façade in one frame. A third option is the road, Sultan Qaboos Street, which gives a complete exterior view that the public entrance by the parking does not.

Keep your photos respectful. Leave worshippers out of the frame and avoid prayer times. The mosque is closed to visitors on Fridays and public holidays, so plan your day around that. Large tripods and drones are typically restricted, so check the current rules on the day. You will not need a tripod anyway, because a phone braced against a wall or held with both hands is fine in daylight.
text.geographic_location: In the Bawshar area of Muscat, on Sultan Qaboos Street (some maps place it in Al Ghubrah). It sits in its own large grounds with a public entrance beside the parking.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed nearby, so from the Bawshar area of Muscat check your local options and travel to the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque public entrance by the parking. Once inside the grounds, walk on to the outer marble courtyard, which is where the phone icon on the map is. Allow a little extra time for the walk within the grounds. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dome and tallest minaret together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the pools and the full façade, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and minaret detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the central dome and the tallest minaret rise together above the courtyard, framed against the bright sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome and main minaret on one of the vertical lines, with the marble courtyard filling the lower third. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. For a different view, the long pools show the dome and minarets reflected with the whole façade in one frame, and Sultan Qaboos Street gives a full exterior view from the road, but use that roadside stop with care.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. Live Photos is useful for capturing a moment without worshippers in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit outside Fridays and public holidays, when the mosque is closed to visitors, and avoid prayer times. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone.

text.access_note: A mosque in active use, closed to visitors on Fridays and public holidays, so check the official site before you go for current visiting times and rules.

name: Muttrah Souq
label: Muttrah Souq
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'سوق مطرح' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'سوق مطرح' (way/35683630): middle (313 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19164055: large area 'Matrah Province' (16344 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic covered market with lanterns, frankincense and textiles.

text.description:
Muttrah Souq is the old market of narrow, shaded lanes beside Muttrah's harbour, and the Corniche entrance is the best way to start photographing it. Locals call it Al Dhalam, meaning "darkness", because its crowded stalls and narrow lanes keep the sun out during the day. It is one of the oldest marketplaces in Oman, around two hundred years old, and it once did a great deal of trade in the age of sail. The market was originally built from mud and palm leaves, and the Muscat Municipality has since renovated and redecorated it.

The domed, arched gateway is the picture to take first. It has an ornate design, and the Corniche and the harbour sit behind it. Inside, the lanes are dim and busy. You will find silver, white dishdashas, embroidered kumahs, bright cloth, incense and spices, and the smell of frankincense and perfume oils carries a long way. These make good close-up subjects: a stall front, a hanging lantern or a pile of colourful scarves.

Go early in the morning if you can. The entrance lanes get crowded in the afternoon and evening, and the market is busiest of all around Eid. If you want a wider view, the Muttrah Fort looks down over the souq roofs, the harbour and the curve of the Corniche. Riyam Park gives you the incense burner monument with the waterfront behind it, but that is a backdrop rather than a view of the souq itself.
text.geographic_location: Muttrah Souq is in Muttrah, the old harbour district of Muscat, right beside the harbour and the Corniche. The gateway photographed here is on the Corniche side.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so reach Muttrah Corniche by road. Ask for the souq entrance and get out opposite the pedestrian traffic lights. The gateway stands right there, and the harbour and the Corniche lie behind it as you face it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole gateway with the Corniche and harbour around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for details on the arch and for stall goods.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Corniche entrance, opposite the pedestrian traffic lights). The domed, arched gateway into the souq, framed by the Corniche and the harbour behind it. From there the camera sees the domed, arched gateway framed by the Corniche, with the harbour behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the gateway centred, holding the phone level so the arch does not lean. Wait for a gap in the pedestrians if you want a clean shot, or keep a few people in to show scale. For a higher view, the Muttrah Fort looks over the souq roofs and harbour, and it is worth checking its access first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the gateway, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and arch keep their detail. Inside the shaded lanes, tap on a stall to focus and raise the exposure slightly, or try night mode if the phone offers it. Hold the phone still for a moment while it works.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up and while the light is good on the gateway's detail.

text.access_note: The gateway can be photographed from the public Corniche, but check current opening hours before you go, as the hours found online come from an old page.
claims_not_in_sources: Shopkeepers and shoppers generally appreciate being asked before close-up portraits.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit a whole gateway into frame when standing close to it.
Night mode may help in dim lanes if the phone offers it.

name: Royal Opera House Muscat
label: Royal Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Kharijiyah Street' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Wadi al Khuwair Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/137570071: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Opera House Muscat' (333 m across).

text.description:
The Royal Opera House Muscat is Oman's main venue for opera, orchestral music and ballet. It opened on 12 October 2011 with a production of Turandot. The building is in contemporary Omani style, with a white marble and pink limestone facade and entrance arches. It sits behind formal landscaped gardens and a paved plaza, and holds up to 1,100 people. The complex also has a concert theatre, a cultural market and an art centre. Sultan Qaboos ordered it built in 2001.

It photographs well because of its scale and its lighting. A close-up from the forecourt cannot show the whole building, but stepping back along the street gives a wider view of its size and its night lights. For this spot the suggested view is from Al Kharijiyah Street, which is the building's street address. In daylight the pale facade is easy to read against the sky. After dark the lit building stands out against the dark. If you want other angles, the plaza in front shows the full facade and entrance arches. The gardens let you frame the building through date palms, water features and walkways, and are usually quieter. Keep your photos to the outside. Photography inside the auditorium is restricted, and tours only allow it in certain areas.
text.geographic_location: The opera house is in the Shati Al-Qurm district of Muscat, on Sultan Qaboos Street, with its street address on Al Kharijiyah Street.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is given for this spot, so the easiest way is by taxi from Shati Al-Qurm, the district the opera house is in. That is a long walk, so a short taxi ride is more practical. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) and use the longest zoom your phone gives cleanly. The default lens (1x) will show the building as a tiny shape in the distance, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) is not useful from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Kharijiyah Street (a stretch of the street some distance from the building, for a wider angle). The building set back along the street, giving a wider view that takes in its scale and the night lighting. From this distance the building will look fairly small, so think of it as a distant view rather than a close portrait. Al Kharijiyah Street is the general stretch of street associated with this view rather than a fixed spot, so choose the exact place by eye, where you have a clear line towards the building and some pavement to stand on safely.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the building on one of the upper lines, with the street or open space leading towards it. Check the vertical edges of the building are straight so it doesn't lean. If you want a bigger, clearer view, the plaza in front gives the full facade and entrance arches. The gardens give a quieter shot through the date palms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights don't burn out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady, for example braced against a wall or post, for the few seconds it needs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: At night, when the building is lit.

text.access_note: The outside of the building can be viewed free of charge, but interior photography is restricted and the building has been closed on some holidays, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: At the distance of the stand-here point the building will look fairly small in a phone photo, so the telephoto lens may help.
Bracing the phone against a wall or post helps keep night photos sharp.

name: Al Alam Palace
label: Al Alam Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Alam Palace' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/66647557: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Al Alam Palace' (269 m across).
notes: The ceremonial palace of the Sultan, with blue and gold columns facing the sea.

text.description: Al Alam Palace is the ceremonial palace of the Sultan of Oman, and its name means "Palace of the Flag". It is used for official functions such as welcoming foreign dignitaries. It is a good stop for phone photos because the front is bold and very symmetrical: gold and blue columns line the facade, and the main gate sits right in the middle. It stands between two old Portuguese-built forts, Al-Mirani and Al-Jalali, which add character to a wider view. The current palace was commissioned by Sultan Qaboos bin Said and finished in 1972, after an earlier palace on the same site was demolished in 1971. The palace sits at the north end of a long arcaded plaza that faces the National Museum of Oman, so there is room to step back and fit more in. The inner grounds are off limits, but visitors may stop near the gates and take photographs, so plan on shooting from outside. Please don't photograph any security staff. The forecourt has little shade at midday, so bring water and a hat if you visit then. For a different view, try the Muttrah Corniche across the harbour, or Al Jalali Fort for a panorama from above, though entry rules there need checking.
text.geographic_location: In Muscat, between Al-Mirani Fort and Al Jalali Fort, at the north end of the arcaded plaza facing the National Museum of Oman.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station information is available for this spot, so use the map to find your way. The palace is at the north end of the arcaded plaza that faces the National Museum of Oman. The phone icon on the map is at the palace itself, so you can use the map to find the front gate. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full facade with the columns and gate, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the columns and the gold-and-blue colours.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand at the front forecourt, centred on the main wrought-iron gate. From the forecourt you get a symmetrical, wide view of the blue-and-gold columns framing the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put yourself on the centre line of the gate and turn on gridlines so the palace sits level and balanced. Keep your phone straight and upright to avoid leaning walls. If you step back along the central walkway, the forts on the cliffs come into view. As an alternative, the Muttrah Corniche shows the palace across the harbour, and Al Jalali Fort gives a view of the whole palace from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate or columns to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the gold detail isn't washed out. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early morning, when the light is softer; one guide suggests the hour around sunset. Midday is bright and the forecourt has little shade.

text.access_note: The palace interior is closed and the inner grounds are off limits, but the public may stop near the gates to take photographs; check the official site before you go for current access.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep a symmetrical building level in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slightly helps stop bright sky and gold details from washing out.
Taking several frames helps when people walk into the shot.

name: Muttrah Fort
label: Muttrah Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mutrah Fort' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Mutrah Fort' (node/4668850593): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM W284633867 (Mutrah Fort): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop fort with panoramic views of the Corniche and harbour.

text.description:
Muttrah Fort stands on a hill above the Corniche, and the best photo of it is taken from the fort itself. The top ramparts and battlements look out over the harbour and the bay. From up there you can fit in the water, the dhows, the Muttrah Corniche and the souq rooftops, with the fort's stone towers in the foreground and the mountains behind. Several guides treat the top of the fort as the standard photo spot. Its height gives the widest panorama in the district, and the view is often at its best in sunset light.

The stone walls give you natural frames and strong lines. Stand close to a battlement and let the towers fill one side of the picture, with the harbour opening out on the other. This works well with a phone because you can take one wide view, then step in for details such as boats, rooftops and the curve of the waterfront.

The fort top is a ticketed viewpoint, and opening hours can vary. The fort may close in the afternoon and may not be open at sunset. If you are planning a sunset photo, check the opening hours on the day before you go. If you can't get in, the Muttrah Corniche is a good second choice. From the waterfront promenade you can photograph the fort on its hill, with boats and the harbour in front and the mountains behind.
text.geographic_location: Muttrah Fort is in the Muttrah district of Muscat, on a hill above the Corniche waterfront and the harbour. The souq rooftops are visible from the fort.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Muttrah Corniche and the souq area. The fort is the stone building on the hill above the waterfront promenade, and you can see it from along the Corniche. The top ramparts inside the fort are a separate recommended viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the ramparts to fit in the harbour, the Corniche and the mountains. Use the default lens (1x) for the fort's towers and walls. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out dhows, souq rooftops and the Corniche below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (top ramparts and battlements, looking out over the harbour and the bay). The harbour, dhows, Mutrah Corniche and souq rooftops framed against the fort's stone towers, with the mountains behind, often in sunset light. Go up onto Mutrah Fort and stand on the top ramparts, by the battlements. From the ramparts the photo shows the harbour, dhows, Mutrah Corniche and souq rooftops framed against the fort's stone towers, with the mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use a battlement or tower as a frame on one side and leave the bay open on the other. Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on a line, with the harbour in the lower part of the picture. Try the same view once wide, then once zoomed in on the boats. If you can't go up, the Muttrah Corniche is a good alternative: it shows the fort on its hill above the promenade, with boats and the harbour in front and the mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone of the towers to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sunset sky keeps its colour. For a sweeping view use panorama mode and hold the phone steady, as moving boats may look blurred or odd in a panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset, when guides say the stone and water catch golden light. Check the fort's closing time on the day.

text.access_note: The top of the fort is a ticketed viewpoint, so check the opening hours and entry details before you go.

name: Bait Al Zubair
label: Bait Al Zubair
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bait al Bagh' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bait al Bagh' (node/4483330544): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3329080: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Museum of Omani heritage in a traditional house with a garden.

text.description: Bait Al Zubair is a museum on Al Saidiya Street in Old Muscat, set in a restored Omani house. It is best known for its collection of old weapons, including khanjar daggers, plus household objects and traditional costumes, much of it from the owner's private collection. For a phone photographer the most rewarding part is outdoors. The garden holds a scale-model Omani village, and the Bait al Bagh area has barasti huts, traditional houses and painted oryx sculptures. Together they make a warm, textured heritage backdrop that suits both wide scene-setting shots and close-ups. The Bait al Bagh village is a recommended viewpoint inside the museum grounds, where you can shoot the huts and houses with the sculptures in the foreground. The restored house front, with its carved doors and windows, is the second picture to get. It looks best from a little way back, so the doors and windows sit inside the old-town setting. A third option is the outer wall and entrance gate seen from Al Saidiya Street, with the courtyard greenery showing beyond. Photography inside the buildings is restricted or banned according to several guides, and flash is limited almost everywhere, so plan your pictures around the outdoor areas. Go in the morning if you can, when the light is softer and it is quieter.
text.geographic_location: The stand-here point is about 284 m south-west of the museum on Al Saidiya Street in Old Muscat.
text.directions_text: No stations or stops are listed nearby, so use the address: Al Saidiya Street, Old Muscat, Bait Al Zubair. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the huts and houses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) in tighter corners, or to 2x-3x telephoto for carved doors and the details on the oryx sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Bait al Bagh (outdoor village area inside the museum grounds, with the painted oryx sculptures). The outdoor Omani village with barasti huts and traditional houses, giving a heritage-village backdrop. Go to Bait al Bagh, the outdoor village inside the museum grounds. From the village you can photograph the barasti huts and traditional houses with the painted oryx sculptures close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put an oryx sculpture or a hut doorway in the foreground and let the village fill the background. Switch on gridlines to keep the rooflines straight. As an alternative, photograph the restored house front with its carved doors and windows from a little way back, or the outer wall and gate from Al Saidiya Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a shaded wall or doorway to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the hut roofs. Keep flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mornings, when the light is soft and the crowds are smaller.

text.access_note: The museum is privately run and ticketed, and the outdoor garden and village are inside the paid grounds; photography inside the buildings is restricted, so check the official site for opening days and photo rules before you go.

name: National Museum of Oman
label: National Museum
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 40 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 120 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/269436905: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum' (120 m across).
notes: Modern museum near Al Alam Palace covering Omani history.

text.description: The National Museum of Oman is the country's flagship cultural museum, and it tells Oman's story from the first human settlement, some two million years ago, up to the present day. It was set up by royal decree in 2013 and opened to the public on 30 July 2016. The building was designed for the job and covers 13,700 square metres, so it is a big, calm subject for a phone photo. Inside are 14 permanent galleries, with themes such as maritime history, arms and armour, the aflaj irrigation systems and Islamic art. The collection numbers 5,466 objects. For a visitor with a phone, the main picture is the whole building seen from outside. Take one wide shot of the full frontage, then a closer one of a single section, such as an entrance or a strong line of the wall. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines, because a large, plain building shows tilted verticals straight away. Wait a moment for people to move out of the way, or include one or two to give a sense of scale. If you go inside, photography rules may differ from the outside, so ask at the entrance.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Old Muscat, in the heart of the city, in a purpose-designed building.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stops are listed nearby, so head for Old Muscat and use a taxi or other local transport. Ask to be dropped at the National Museum of Oman. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole building in, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If you want a detail such as an entrance or a wall pattern, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Al Alam Square (across the square from the museum, facing the building). The museum's front facade across the open square, with the mountains visible behind it on clear days. Walk a few steps left or right until the building looks square to you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roofline or the base of the building with a horizontal grid line, so the walls stay upright. Take one wide shot of the whole building. Then take a second, tighter shot with the default lens (1x) or the telephoto, picking out one section with strong lines. Include a person at the edge of the frame if you want to show how large it is.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail rather than washing out. Hold the phone with both hands and keep it level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls than the middle of the day. After dusk, night mode can work if the building is lit, but rest your elbows on something steady.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the surrounding area, but entry to the galleries and any photography rules inside should be checked on the official site before you go.

name: Al-Mirani Fort
label: Mirani Fort
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 4 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 15 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/178157862: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fort Al-Mirani' (138 m across).
notes: Portuguese fort on the opposite headland, facing Jalali across the harbour.

text.description:
Al-Mirani Fort stands over the harbour in Old Muscat, on the Muscat waterfront. It is a compact fort on rising ground, with a water backdrop and rugged hills close by. That gives you a layered picture even on a quick visit. The walls and towers have a solid, sandy look that stands out well against a clear sky.

The fort was already here before the Portuguese arrived, and they rebuilt it in 1587. It is described as the first fort in Oman to use cannons. In 1552 an Ottoman force of 4 galleons, 25 galleys and 850 troops captured Muscat. The recently built fort was besieged for 18 days before it fell and its fortifications were destroyed. It is worth remembering this when you frame your shot, as the walls you see are part of a long story.

For a phone photo, stand. The fort's centre is about 59 m to the south, which puts you at or near the edge of the fort, so the whole building may not fit in one frame from here. Start with the default lens (1x) so the fort sits in its harbour setting. Then try the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the towers and wall texture. If you cannot fit it all in, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) or shoot the fort in sections, but keep the fort away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched. Turn on gridlines to keep the walls level.
text.geographic_location: Al-Mirani Fort is in the harbour of Old Muscat, on the Muscat waterfront in Oman.
text.directions_text: Head for the harbour area of Old Muscat; no station or tram stop serves this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the fort in its harbour setting. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the towers and walls, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the whole fort will not fit in one frame from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Al Alam Palace Gardens. The fort framed across the palace grounds, with the harbour and sea behind it, and Al Jalali Fort visible alongside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the fort's horizon line level with a horizontal grid line. Leave some sky above the towers and some of the harbour or foreground below to give a sense of place. Take one wide shot, then step forward and take a tighter one with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. A Live Photo can catch movement in the harbour if boats pass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls than the middle of the day.

text.access_note: Access to the fort itself may be restricted or ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Al Jalali Fort
label: Jalali Fort
pin_note: Position from OSM R2690780 (Al Jalali Fort): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A 16th-century Portuguese fort on a rocky headland above Muscat harbour.

text.description:
Al Jalali Fort is one of the spots on the Muscat map, and this spot shows it from a distance rather than from its gates. That suits a phone well. It reads as a single solid shape, with the walls and towers set against the sky and the surrounding rock, instead of a close-up of stonework. Seen from here you can fit the whole building into the frame, which is hard to do once you are right beneath it.

At this distance the fort will look small at the default lens (1x), so use the telephoto or zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring it closer. Try a wide frame first with the fort sitting in the landscape, then a tighter one that fills the frame with the towers and walls. Turn on the gridlines and place the fort on one of the lines so that it does not sit dead centre. Keep the horizon level, because a tilted horizon is very obvious with a long straight wall in the picture.

If the air is hazy, tap the fort to focus and pull the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the walls. Take a few shots in a row, as zoomed pictures blur easily when your hands move. Look at the official site for the fort's history and visiting rules before you plan a visit inside.
text.geographic_location: Al Jalali Fort is in Muscat.
text.directions_text: Walk east and keep the fort in view as you go. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a wide view that shows the fort in its surroundings. Then switch to the telephoto or zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer view of the walls and towers. Avoid the ultra-wide (0.5x), which would make the fort tiny.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Al Mirani Fort (foot of the fort, on the opposite (western) side of the harbour). The twin fort across the harbour, showing Al Jalali's full structure on its rocky outcrop against the sea. Stay in the same spot for both the wide and the zoomed pictures.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the fort on one of the lines. Leave some sky above the towers and keep the horizon straight. Take one wide shot with the fort in its setting, then a zoomed one filling the frame with the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fort to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its colour. Hold the phone with both hands when zooming, and take a few frames to get one sharp one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and gives the walls more shape. Midday sun is harsher and flatter.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for access to the fort itself. This viewing spot is a short walk away from it.
claims_not_in_sources: The fort will look small at the default lens (1x) from about 400 metres away.

name: Riyam Incense Burner
label: Incense Burner
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riyam Park' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Riyam Amusement Park' (pois).

notes: Giant incense burner monument on a hill above the bay at Riyam Park.

text.description:
The Riyam Incense Burner is a giant white incense burner standing on a hilltop in Riyam, a village in Muscat, in northeastern Oman. It is a simple, bold shape, and the hill gives it open sky behind it. From the park's paths and elevated spots, you can fit the whole sculpture into one frame at a distance, with the sea, the city and the surrounding mountains behind it. That layered backdrop is what makes the picture work.

The best views come from the park's paths and the slightly raised areas around the monument. Walk along until you find a spot with a clear line of sight, because trees and railings can get in the way in some places. Access to the monument itself is restricted, so photograph it from the park rather than close up, and please don't climb on it or damage it. Photography of the monument is allowed.

A second option is Mutrah Corniche, where the burner appears small on its hill above the waterfront and harbour. It is a street-level view from a distance, so it suits a wider scene rather than a detailed shot of the sculpture.

The white surface can look washed out in strong sun, so check your screen before moving on. Sunset or golden hour gives softer colour on the sculpture, and it is lit up at night, which makes a good second visit if you are staying nearby.
text.geographic_location: The monument stands on a hill in Riyam, a village in Muscat, with Riyam Park around and below it. It looks out over the Mutrah waterfront and harbour.
text.directions_text: Head for Riyam Park in Muscat. Choose a path with a clear view up to the hilltop. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the sculpture, sea and city into one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it to bring the burner closer from the park without leaving the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Riyam Park (pathways and elevated areas within the park, below and around the monument). The giant white incense burner on its hilltop, framed against the sea, the city and the surrounding mountains. Look south-east to see the white incense burner on its hilltop, framed against the sea, the city and the mountains. Move along the nearby park paths until you have a clear line of sight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the burner on one of the vertical lines, with the sea or city filling the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. Hold the phone low and tilt slightly upwards so the hilltop looks tall without cutting off the base. For a different view, try Mutrah Corniche, where the monument appears as a landmark above the harbour.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white sculpture to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the surface keeps its detail. At night, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset or golden hour for soft light. The monument is lit at night, so you can also try it after dark.

text.access_note: The park is a public space, but access to the monument itself is restricted and opening hours can vary, so check on the day before you go.

label: Muscat Gate Museum

notes: The old city gate of Muscat, now a small museum.

text.description:
Muscat Gate Museum sits in the modern gate that marks the entrance to Old Muscat. The structure was built in 1995, and the museum inside opened in January 2001. It tells Oman's story from the Neolithic period to today, with a focus on how Muscat grew from a trading port into a modern capital. The gate stands on Al Saidiya Street, and its arch is a handy frame for photos. The old walled city's gates were once closed before sundown.

For photos, the best-liked moment is the view from the upper level on top of the gate. From there you look over the sea and the rooftops of Mutrah and old Muscat, with the top of the gate itself in the foreground, which adds depth to a simple shot. A second option is to photograph the arched gate and museum block with the road in front and the rugged hills behind. That gives you a sense of the gate's place at the edge of the old town.

Check the road around you before you step back for a wider shot. The museum has been reported closed on some visits, so the top-of-gate view may not always be available. Check opening times before you go, and have the arch-and-hills view ready as your back-up.
text.geographic_location: Muscat Gate Museum is on Al Saidiya Street, at the entrance to Old Muscat. It sits above the modern gate and looks towards the old town and Mutrah.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot. The gate stands on Al Saidiya Street at the entrance to Old Muscat. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the gate and the view from the top, because it takes in the arch and the townscape together. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural look at the arch or the museum block. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out rooftops and the sea in Mutrah.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the sea and the Mutrah and old Muscat townscape from above, with the top of the gate in the foreground. If the top is closed, stand by the gate itself, where you can take the arched gate and museum block against the road and the hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Place part of the gate's top edge or parapet in the foreground and let the town and sea fill the rest of the frame. Switch on gridlines and set the horizon on a top or bottom line so it stays level. As an alternative, shoot the arched gate and museum block with the road in front and the rugged hills behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the town to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the buildings keep their colour. Wipe the lens before you shoot, as it picks up dust easily.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually more comfortable and gives softer light. Opening can be unreliable, so check opening times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a museum on top of a gate, and the museum has been reported closed on some visits, so check opening and entry details before you go.
